content.text:
**Finding: Compliant** — no redline proposed.

Section 20 of the MSA already reaches our preferred playbook position on vendor indemnification:

| Playbook requirement | Where satisfied |
|---|---|
| Vendor IP infringement indemnity for Services/Deliverables | 20.1 — unqualified, no modification/combination exclusions |
| Extends to Customer affiliates | 20.1 — Customer, Affiliates, directors, officers, employees, agents (Affiliate broadly defined at 1.1) |
| Vendor breach of law | 20.2 |
| Data breach caused by Vendor | 20.2 — unauthorised access to or disclosure of Customer Data |
| Gross negligence / wilful misconduct | 20.2 — plus fraud and bodily injury/property damage (better than model) |
| Standard procedure (notice, control, cooperation) | 20.4 — material-prejudice qualifier on notice, cooperation at indemnitor's expense, no prejudicial settlement without consent |
| Customer indemnity stays narrow | 20.3 — only unmodified Customer material used strictly as authorised and Customer's own breach of law, with carve-outs for Vendor Technology, modifications, combinations, Vendor instructions |

Two additional points worth noting in our favour:

- **20.5** gives the procure/modify/replace/refund remedies but expressly says they are *in addition to* Vendor's defence obligation, and bars Vendor from terminating unaffected Services. This is why we land at preferred rather than the fallback — the remedies are not a substitute for the indemnity.
- **21.3** confirms indemnification obligations, gross negligence/wilful misconduct/fraud, and IP infringement are all "Excluded Claims" sitting outside the mutual cap in 21.1, so the fallback's 3× annual fees super-cap is unnecessary.

One item outside this rule's scope that a liability-focused review should pick up: the cap in **21.1** is measured against fees "under the **first Order Form**" rather than all fees paid under the Agreement, which could understate our recovery in a multi-order relationship. That does not affect indemnity claims (they are Excluded Claims), so I have left it for the limitation-of-liability rule.
